paragraphs.heading: What they are
paragraphs.text: Greenhouse gases are the gases in an atmosphere that trap heat and so raise the surface temperature of a body such as Earth. Sunlight warms Earth's surface, the surface gives off heat, and greenhouse gases soak up most of that heat; this is the greenhouse effect. Without them, Earth's surface would average about −18 °C (0 °F) instead of today's 15 °C (59 °F).

paragraphs.heading: Why only some gases
paragraphs.text: What sets these gases apart is that they are infrared active: they absorb and give off infrared radiation in the same long wavelengths that Earth's surface, clouds and air emit. Argon, 0.9% of the air, is made of single atoms and lets heat radiation pass straight through. Carbon dioxide (0.04%), methane, nitrous oxide and rarer trace gases add up to less than 0.1% of the atmosphere. But their molecules join atoms of different elements, which makes their electric charge lopsided and lets their vibrations interact with radiation, and that is why they cause a greenhouse effect.

paragraphs.heading: The energy balance
paragraphs.text: Earth absorbs part of the Sun's energy and sends the rest back to space as reflected light or as heat. A planet's surface temperature depends on the balance between energy coming in and energy going out, and when that balance shifts, the surface warms or cools. Such a shift is measured as radiative forcing, in watts per square meter. More greenhouse gas is a positive forcing: more energy arrives than leaves at the top of the atmosphere, so the planet warms.

paragraphs.heading: Water vapor
paragraphs.text: Water vapor is the most important greenhouse gas overall, causing 41–67% of the greenhouse effect. Yet human activity does not directly change how much there is worldwide; irrigation can affect it locally, but vapor stays in the air only about nine days. Instead it responds to the other gases: warmer air holds more water vapor per unit volume, by the Clausius–Clapeyron relation, which adds more warming. This is called water vapor feedback.

paragraphs.heading: What humans have added
paragraphs.text: Since the Industrial Revolution began around 1750, human activity has raised carbon dioxide by over 50% and methane by 150%. Carbon dioxide causes about three-quarters of global warming, and methane most of the rest. Most human CO₂ comes from burning fossil fuels, with agriculture and industry adding the remainder, while methane comes from agriculture, fossil fuel production, waste and other sources. The two linger very differently: methane lasts about 12 years on average, but the carbon cycle needs thousands of years to fully take CO₂ back out of the air.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring the rise
paragraphs.text: The amount of a greenhouse gas is usually stated by volume, as parts per million (ppm) or as parts per billion (ppb). A CO₂ level of 420 ppm means 420 of every million air molecules are CO₂. The first 30 ppm of increase took about 200 years, from the Industrial Revolution to 1958, while the next 90 ppm came in just 56 years, up to 2014. Carbon dioxide levels are now higher than at any time in three million years.

paragraphs.heading: Where this is heading
paragraphs.text: Human-caused warming is now rising faster than at any time since measurements began, reaching 0.27±0.1 °C each decade during 2015–2024. If emissions keep going at today's rates, warming will go beyond 2.0 °C (3.6 °F) at some point from 2040 to 2070. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) calls that level dangerous.
